raw_response:
Ai, where do I start. I've been working this dirt for fifty years, since I was a boy following my father with a hoe. My back tells me the years now, and at home it's just me and the old lady — both kids went south for factory work years ago. We've got 57 mu, which is a lot for two old people, but I can't bear to let it sit. So for the heavy jobs — plowing, planting the maize, harvesting the wheat — I just call the machine man from the village. He charges by the mu, comes through, done in a day. That's how everyone does it now.

Most of the land, maybe 54 mu, I keep in wheat and maize like always. Wheat in October after the maize comes off, then maize again in June right after the combine cuts the wheat. That's the rhythm, never changes. Then I keep about 3 mu near the house in scallion (大葱) — the old lady and me can just about manage that much by hand, and it brings in real cash when the traders come through in autumn. More scallion than that and we'd kill ourselves.

For the wheat, I do what I've always done. Before planting I spread compound fertilizer — about one bag (50 jin, so 25 kg) per mu of the 复合肥, the kind with all three numbers on it. The shop owner knows what I want. Then in spring when the wheat starts standing up tall — what they call jointing — I broadcast urea, maybe half a bag per mu, around 20 jin (10 kg). If the wheat looks yellow I put down a bit more, if it looks dark green I hold back. My eyes know. Three or four waterings through the season — first one before winter to settle the soil, then at jointing, then when the heads are filling. Water from the well costs money for the electric, so I don't waste it. If it rains good I skip a watering.

Maize is simpler. After the wheat combine goes through, the planter comes right behind and drops seed and fertilizer together — another bag of compound per mu mixed in. Tight window, can't be lazy. Maize doesn't need much water if the rains come in July-August like they should. Maybe one watering if July goes dry. I spray once for armyworms if I see them on the leaves, and once for weeds early on.

Scallion is where the real work and money go. We start the seedlings in the small bed in early spring, transplant them in May into the deep furrows. That land gets heavy fertilizer — I dump manure from the village pig farm if I can get it, plus several bags of compound through the season. Water it often, every week or so when it's hot. Spray for the white worm (onion maggot) and for downy mildew — the agro-shop man tells me what to buy, I just trust him. By October-November the scallions are tall and white at the base, that's when the traders come and we pull them.

I don't keep books. I know roughly what I spent because I remember what bags I bought. Last year was a normal year, so I'll do about the same this year. If the wheat price stays low I might think about more scallion next year, but at my age I'm not making big changes.
